readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|The clay [Bow porcelain], which was called ''unaker'', was brought from America, and was probably an impure kind of kaolin.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIX. 641.}}}}
'''unalienable''' (un-āl′yen-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Inalienable. ''Coleridge.'' [Rare.]

'''unalienably''' (un-āl′yen-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' Inalienably. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, iv. [Rare.]

'''unalist†''' (ū′nal-ist), ''n.'' [< L. ''unus'', one (see ''one''), + ''-al-ist'', formed on analogy of ''pluralist.''] ''Eccles.'', a holder of only one benefice: opposed to ''pluralist.'' ''V. Knox'', Spirit of Despotism, § 33. [Rare.]

'''unallayed†''' (un-a̤-lād′), ''a.'' Unalloyed.
{{smaller block|Our happiness is now as ''unallayed'' as general.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, v. 3.}}}}

'''unalliable''' (un-a̤-lī′a-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be allied or connected in amity.
{{smaller block|Perpetual and ''unalliable'' aliens.
{{right|''Burke'', Letter to Sir Henry Langrishe.}}}}

'''unallied''' (un-a̤-līd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no alliance or connection by nature, marriage, or treaty: as, ''unallied'' families, nations, substances.—'''2.''' Having no powerful ally or relation. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, v.

'''unalloyed''' (un-a-loid′), ''a.'' Not alloyed; not debased or reduced by foreign admixture; hence, pure; complete; entire: as, metals ''unalloyed''; ''unalloyed'' satisfaction.

'''unalterability''' (un-âl″tėr-a-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' Unalterableness. ''Ruskin'', Elements of Drawing, p. 145.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unalterable''' (un-âl′tėr-a-bl), ''a.'' Not alterable; unchangeable; immutable.
{{smaller block|The law of nature, consisting in a fixed ''unalterable'' relation of one nature to another. {{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}}

'''unalterableness''' (un-âl′tėr-a-bl-nes), ''n.'' Unchangeableness; immutability. ''J. Edwards'', Works, IV. 185.

'''unalterably''' (un-âl′tėr-a-bli), ''adv.'' Unchangeably; immutably. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 502.

'''unaltered''' (un-âl′tėrd), ''a.'' Not altered or changed.
{{smaller block|Keep an even and ''unaltered'' gait. {{right|''B. Jonson'', The Forest.}}}}

'''unambiguous''' (un-am-big′ū-us), ''a.'' Not ambiguous; not of doubtful meaning; plain; perspicuous; clear; certain.

'''unambiguously''' (un-am-big′ū-us-li), ''adv.'' In a manner not ambiguous; without ambiguity; plainly; clearly.

'''unambitious''' (un-am-bish′us), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not ambitious; free from ambition; not marked by ambition.
{{smaller block|My humble muse, in ''unambitious'' strains. {{right|''Pope'', Windsor Forest.}}}}
'''2.''' Not affecting show; not showy or prominent; unpretending: as, ''unambitious'' ornaments.

'''unambitiously''' (un-am-bish′us-li), ''adv.'' In an unambitious manner; without ambition. ''Wordsworth'', Excursion, vii.

'''unamendable''' (un-a-men′da-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being amended or corrected. ''Pope'', Letter to Swift, Oct. 9, 1719.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unamusing''' (un-a̤-mū′zing), ''a.'' Not amusing. ''Athenæum'', No. 3301, p. 150.

'''unamusingly''' (un-a̤-mū′zing-li), ''adv.'' In an unamusing manner. ''Athenæum'', No. 3254, p. 316.

'''unamusive''' (un-ạ-mū′ziv), ''a.'' Not affording or characterized by amusement. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I have passed a very dull and ''unamusive'' winter.
{{right|''Shenstone'', Letters, I. 83. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''unancestried''' (un-an′ses-trid), ''a.'' Not having a distinguished ancestry. ''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 163. [Rare.]

'''unanchor''' (un-ang′kọr), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''anchor''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To loose from anchorage.
{{smaller block|Kate will have free elbow-room for ''unanchoring'' her boat.
{{right|''De Quincey'', Spanish Nun, § 5. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become loose from anchorage; become detached. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It soon comes in contact with a colony of the organism in the perfectly flagellate condition, attaches itself to one of them, which soon ''unanchors'', and both swim away.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', Aug., 1878, p. 511.}}}}

'''unanealed†''', '''unaneled†''' (un-ạ-nēld′), ''a.'' Not having received extreme unction. See ''aneal''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|Unhousel’d, disappointed, ''unaneled''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5. 77.}}}}

'''unangular''' (un-ang′gū-lär), ''a.'' Not angular; having no angles. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Soft, smooth, ''unangular'' bodies.
{{right|''Burke'', On the Sublime and Beautiful, § 24.}}}}

'''unanimalized''' (un-an′i-mạl-īzd), ''a.'' Not formed into animal matter.
readings.c3s1:

'''unanimate<sup>1</sup>''' (un-an′i-māt), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''animate.''] Inanimate. ''Tomkis'' (?), Albumazar, ii. 5. [Rare.]

'''unanimate<sup>2</sup>†''' (ū-nan′i-māt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unanimus'', of one mind (see ''unanimous''), + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Of one mind; unanimous. [Rare.]

'''unanimated''' (un-an′i-mā-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not animated; not possessed of life. ''Dryden'', Æneid, Ded.—'''2.''' Not enlivened; not having spirit; dull; inanimate.

'''unanimately†''' (ū-nan′i-māt-li), ''adv.'' [< ''unanimate''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Unanimously.
{{smaller block|To the water foules ''unanimately'' they recourse.
{{right|''Nashe'', Lenten Stuffe (Harl. Misc., VI. 170). (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unanimity''' (ū-na-nim′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< F. ''unanimité'' = Sp. ''unanimidad'' = Pg. ''unanimidade'' = It. ''unanimità'', < LL. ''unanimita(t-)s'', < L. ''unanimus'', ''unanimis'', unanimous: see ''unanimous.''] The state of being unanimous; agreement in opinion or resolution of all the persons concerned.
{{smaller block|Where they do agree on the stage, their ''unanimity'' is wonderful.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Critic, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unanimous''' (ū-nan′i-mus), ''a.'' [= F. ''unanime'' = Sp. ''unanime'' = Pg. ''unanime'' = It. ''unanime'', ''unanimo'', < L. ''unanimus'', ''unanimis'', of one mind, < ''unus'', one, + ''animus'', mind: see ''animus.''] '''1.''' Being of one mind; agreeing in opinion or determination; consentient.
{{smaller block|Both in one faith ''unanimous.''
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 603.}}}}
'''2.''' Formed with unanimity; exhibiting unanimity: as, a ''unanimous'' vote.

{{smaller block|financial opposition to tyranny is apt to be ''unanimous.''
{{right|''Motley'', Dutch Republic, II. 285.}}}}

¶
'''unanimously''' (ū-nan′i-mus-li), ''adv.'' With one mind or voice; with unanimity. ''Jer. Taylor'', Of the Real Presence, § 3.

'''unanimousness''' (ū-nan′i-mus-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unanimous.

'''unanswerability''' (un-ȧn″sėr-a̤-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' Unanswerableness.

'''unanswerable''' (un-ȧn′sėr-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be satisfactorily answered; not susceptible of refutation: as, an ''unanswerable'' argument. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Irrefutable, irrefragable, incontrovertible.}}

'''unanswerableness''' (un-ȧn′sėr-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unanswerable.

'''unanswerably''' (un-ȧn′sėr-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a manner not to be answered; beyond refutation. ''Jer. Taylor'', Rule of Conscience, iii. 3.

'''unanswered''' (un-ȧn′sėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not answered; not replied to; not opposed by a reply: as, an ''unanswered'' letter.
{{smaller block|<poem>Must I tamely bear
This arrogance ''unanswer’d?'' Thou ’rt a traitor.</poem>
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
'''2.''' Not refuted: as, an ''unanswered'' argument. —'''3.''' Not suitably returned; unrequited.
{{smaller block|Quench, Corydon, thy long ''unanswer’d'' fire.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ii. 105.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''unanxious''' (un-angk′shus), ''a.'' Free from anxiety. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, i. [Rare.]

'''unapostolic''' (un-ap-ọs-tol′ik), ''a.'' Not apostolic; not agreeable to apostolic usage; not having apostolic authority.

'''unapostolical''' (un-ap-ọs-tol′i-kạl), ''a.'' Same as ''unapostolic.''

'''unappalled''' (un-ạ-pâld′), ''a.'' Not appalled; not daunted; not impressed with fear; dauntless. ''Milton'', P. R., iv. 425.

'''unapparel''' (un-ạ-par′el), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unappareled'', ''unapparelled'', ppr. ''unappareling'', ''unapparelling''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''apparel.''] To uncover; undress; unclothe; disclose.
{{smaller block|Ladies, ''unapparel'' your dear beauties.
{{right|''Middleton'', Blurt, Master-Constable, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unappareled, unapparelled''' (un-a̤-par′eld), ''a.'' Not wearing clothes; habitually unclothed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They were ''unapparelled'' people, according to the clime, and had some customs very barbarous. ''Bacon'', Holy War.}}

'''unapparent''' (un-a̤-pãr′ẹnt), ''a.'' Not apparent; obscure; not visible.
{{smaller block|Bitter actions of despite, too subtle and too ''unapparent'' for law to deal with. {{right|''Milton'', Tetrachordon.}}

The Zoroastrian definition of poetry, mystical, yet exact, “apparent pictures of ''unapparent'' natures.”
{{right|''Emerson'', Complete Prose Works, II. 276.}}}}
readings.c3s4:
¶
'''unappealable''' (un-a̤-pē′la̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not appealable; incapable of being carried to a higher court by appeal: as, an ''unappealable'' cause. —'''2.''' Not to be appealed from; final: as, an ''unappealable'' judge. ''South'', Sermons, V. iii.

'''unappeasable''' (un-a̤-pē′za̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be appeased or pacified; implacable: as, ''unappeasable'' anger. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 963.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unadvisedness|6579|unappeasable}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''unadvisedness''' (un-ad-vī′zẹd-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unadvised; imprudence; rashness; indiscretion.
{{smaller block|''Unadvisedness'' coupled with heedlessness, and mis-advisedness coupled with rashness, correspond to the culpa sine dolo.
{{right|''Bentham'', Introd. to Morals and Legislation, ix. 17.}}}}

'''unaffable''' (un-af′ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not affable; reserved. ''Daniel'', To Sir T. Egerton.

'''unaffeared''' (un-ạ-fērd′), ''a.'' Not frightened; not afraid. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, iii. 76.

'''unaffected''' (un-ạ-fek′ted), ''a.'' Not affected. {{smaller|(''a'') Not acted upon; not influenced; not altered.}}
{{smaller block|The same ''unaffected'', unbiassed, unbribable, unaffrighted innocence. {{right|''Emerson'', Essays, p. 47.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not moved; not having the heart or passions touched; destitute of affection or emotion.}}
{{smaller block|A poor, cold, unspirited, . . . ''unaffected'' fool.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Not showing affectation; plain; natural; not artificial; simple.}}
{{smaller block|A wise, sober, seemly, ''unaffected'' deportment.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Sermon, Eccles. iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') Real; not pretended; sincere: as, ''unaffected'' sorrow.}}

'''unaffectedly''' (un-ạ-fek′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unaffected manner; without affectation, or the attempt to produce false appearances; simply.

'''unaffectedness''' (un-ạ-fek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unaffected. ''Athenæum'', No. 3233, p. 479.

'''unaffied''' (un-ạ-fīd′), ''a.'' Not allied or affianced.
{{smaller block|<poem>Not unrelated, ''unaffied'',
But to each thought and thing allied,
Is perfect Nature’s every part.</poem>
{{right|''Emerson'', Woodnotes, ii.}}}}

'''unaffiled†''' (un-ạ-fīld′), ''a.'' Undefiled.
{{smaller block|<poem>No strength of love bowe might
His herte, whiche is ''unaffiled.''</poem>
{{right|''Gower'', Conf. Amant., i.}}}}

'''unaffrighted''' (un-ạ-frī′ted), ''a.'' Not frightened. ''Fletcher'', Double Marriage, i. 2.

'''unafraid''' (un-ạ-frād′), ''a.'' Not afraid. ''Thomson'', Castle of Indolence, ii. 28. [Rare.]

'''unagreeable''' (un-ạ-grē′a-bl), ''a.'' Not agreeable. {{smaller|(''a'') Not pleasing; disagreeable; distasteful. [Rare.]}}
{{smaller block|Myn unpietous lyf draweth a long ''unagreable'' dwellynges in me.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boethius, i. meter 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not consistent; unsuitable.}}
{{smaller block|The manner of their living ''unagreeable'' to the profession of the names of Christians.
{{right|''E. Knight'', Trial of Truth, fol. 53.}}
The Summer well nigh ending, and the season ''unagreeable'' to transport a Warr.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

'''unagreeableness''' (un-ạ-grē′a-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unagreeable, in either sense. ''Decay of Christian Piety.'' (''Richardson.'')

'''unagreeably''' (un-ạ-grē′a-bli), ''adv.'' Not agreeably. {{smaller|(''a'') Disagreeably. (''b'') Unsuitably; inconsistently.}}

'''unaided''' (un-ā′ded), ''a.'' Not aided; not assisted.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy allies . . . for thy sake . . .
Perish ''unaided'' and unmissed by thee.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, xvi. 652.}}}}

'''unaiming''' (un-ā′ming), ''a.'' Having no particular aim or direction. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The noisy culverin, o’ercharged, lets fly,
And bursts, ''unaiming'', in the rended sky.</poem>
{{right|''Granville.''}}}}

'''unaker†''', ''n.'' See the quotation, and ''Bow porcelain'' (under ''porcelain'').

{{smaller block|The clay [Bow porcelain], which was called ''unaker'', was brought from America, and was probably an impure kind of kaolin.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIX. 641.}}}}
'''unalienable''' (un-āl′yen-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Inalienable. ''Coleridge.'' [Rare.]

'''unalienably''' (un-āl′yen-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' Inalienably. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, iv. [Rare.]

'''unalist†''' (ū′nal-ist), ''n.'' [< L. ''unus'', one (see ''one''), + ''-al-ist'', formed on analogy of ''pluralist.''] ''Eccles.'', a holder of only one benefice: opposed to ''pluralist.'' ''V. Knox'', Spirit of Despotism, § 33. [Rare.]

'''unallayed†''' (un-a̤-lād′), ''a.'' Unalloyed.
{{smaller block|Our happiness is now as ''unallayed'' as general.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, v. 3.}}}}

'''unalliable''' (un-a̤-lī′a-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be allied or connected in amity.

{{smaller block|So far as the law permits such wrongs, it is unequal and ''un-American'' law, by which some men’s rights are wrongfully abridged in order that the privileges of others may be wrongfully enlarged. {{right|''New Princeton Rev.'', IV. 327.}}}}

'''un-Americanize''' (un-ạ-mer′i-kạn-īz), ''v. t.'' To render un-American in character; assimilate to foreign customs and institutions. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Foreign interests and alien population tend to ''un-Americanize'' the place. {{right|''The American'', VII. 117.}}}}

'''unamiability''' (un-ā″mi-a-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unamiable. ''R. Broughton'', Belinda, iv.

'''unamiable''' (un-ā′mi-ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not amiable or lovable; not inducing love; not adapted to gain affection; repelling love or kind advances; ill-natured; repulsive.
{{smaller block|These ladies of irresistible modesty are those who make virtue ''unamiable.'' {{right|''Steele.''}}}}

'''unamused''' (un-a-mūzd′), ''a.'' Not amused; not entertained; not cheered by diversion or relaxation.
{{smaller block|Instead of being ''unamused'' by trifles, I am, as I well know I should be, amused by them a great deal too much. {{right|''Sydney Smith'', to Francis Jeffrey.}}}}

'''unamusingly''' (un-a̤-mū′zing-li), ''adv.'' In an unamusing manner. ''Athenæum'', No. 3254, p. 316.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become loose from anchorage; become detached. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It soon comes in contact with a colony of the organism in the perfectly flagellate condition, attaches itself to one of them, which soon ''unanchors'', and both swim away.

'''unanimousness''' (ū-nan′i-mus-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unanimous.

{{smaller block|Quench, Corydon, thy long ''unanswer’d'' fire.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ii. 105.}}}}

'''unanxious''' (un-angk′shus), ''a.'' Free from anxiety. ''Young'', Night Thoughts, i. [Rare.]

'''unapostolic''' (un-ap-ọs-tol′ik), ''a.'' Not apostolic; not agreeable to apostolic usage; not having apostolic authority.

'''unapostolical''' (un-ap-ọs-tol′i-kạl), ''a.'' Same as ''unapostolic.''

'''unappalled''' (un-ạ-pâld′), ''a.'' Not appalled; not daunted; not impressed with fear; dauntless. ''Milton'', P. R., iv. 425.

'''unapparel''' (un-ạ-par′el), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''unappareled'', ''unapparelled'', ppr. ''unappareling'', ''unapparelling''. [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''apparel.''] To uncover; undress; unclothe; disclose.
{{smaller block|Ladies, ''unapparel'' your dear beauties.
{{right|''Middleton'', Blurt, Master-Constable, ii. 2.}}}}

'''unappareled, unapparelled''' (un-a̤-par′eld), ''a.'' Not wearing clothes; habitually unclothed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They were ''unapparelled'' people, according to the clime, and had some customs very barbarous. ''Bacon'', Holy War.}}

'''unapparent''' (un-a̤-pãr′ẹnt), ''a.'' Not apparent; obscure; not visible.
{{smaller block|Bitter actions of despite, too subtle and too ''unapparent'' for law to deal with. {{right|''Milton'', Tetrachordon.}}

The Zoroastrian definition of poetry, mystical, yet exact, “apparent pictures of ''unapparent'' natures.”
{{right|''Emerson'', Complete Prose Works, II. 276.}}}}

'''unappealable''' (un-a̤-pē′la̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not appealable; incapable of being carried to a higher court by appeal: as, an ''unappealable'' cause. —'''2.''' Not to be appealed from; final: as, an ''unappealable'' judge. ''South'', Sermons, V. iii.

'''unappeasable''' (un-a̤-pē′za̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be appeased or pacified; implacable: as, ''unappeasable'' anger. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 963.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
